details.label: Summary
details.text: The threat for at least isolated severe storms capable of large hail in excess of two inches and severe wind gusts up to 70-80 mph is expected to increase by mid to late afternoon. Convective trends are being monitored for one or multiple severe thunderstorm watches

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Clusters of elevated thunderstorms have persisted so far today from the NE Sandhills into eastern NE with activity potentially being aided by a weak mid-level disturbance moving into northern NE. The 18Z OAX sounding suggests that storms are likely rooted above a relatively dry layer extending from just above the ground to 3-4 km AGL with the presence of steep mid-level lapse rates contributing to MUCAPE of 1500-2500+ J/kg. Considerable uncertainty still exists in storm evolution through the remainder of the afternoon. More recent storm development northeast of McCook, NE is occurring closer to a front-outflow composite boundary, ahead of which temperatures have warmed into the upper 80s to around 90 with steepening low-level lapse rates. That activity may intensify as it continues southeast into a hotter, more unstable air mass in place over northwest and north-central KS. Elsewhere, ongoing elevated thunderstorms from north-central into eastern NE may also intensify through mid/late afternoon amidst a kinematic environment featuring 40-50+ kt of deep-layer shear, which is conditionally supportive of supercell storm modes. The strongest storms will be capable of large hail, potentially in excess of two inches, as well as damaging wind gusts up to 70-80 mph

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Isolated thunderstorms are ongoing across west-central Alabama and southern Georgia as of 1800 UTC, with additional development expected along a remnant outflow boundary and within pockets of modestly enhanced surface convergence across the region through the afternoon. High PW (1.75-2.0+ inches) and steepening low-level lapse rates will foster at least an isolated risk for damaging wind gusts with water-loaded downbursts; however, marginally cooler temperatures (low 90s F) and modestly weaker low-to-mid level flow (less than 15-20 kts per area VWPs) suggest the coverage and magnitude of the severe risk may be somewhat more limited compared to areas farther west. Given this, the need for a Severe Thunderstorm Watch is more uncertain but appears unlikely at this time. Trends will continue to be monitored, and a watch could be considered should a corridor of greater damaging wind gust potential become evident

details.label: Summary
details.text: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms will pose a risk for damaging wind gusts and perhaps isolated marginally severe hail this afternoon and evening. A Severe Thunderstorm Watch may be needed

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Latest surface analysis depicts a cold front extending from northern Mississippi westward along the Arkansas/Louisiana border and into northeastern Texas. This boundary; along with remnant outflow from overnight convection, the coastal sea breeze, and a remnant MCV evident in visible satellite imagery across central Alabama; will serve as a focus for convective initiation this afternoon amid a hot and humid air mass with temperatures in the upper-90s F and dewpoints in the mid-70s F. While effective shear remains generally meager (less than 20 kts per objective analysis and 12z regional observed soundings), modestly stronger low-to-mid level flow (20-25 kts sampled by area VWPs), high PW content (1.75-2.0+ inches), and steepening low-level lapse rates (8-9+ C/km) will support scattered damaging/severe wind gusts with water-loaded downbursts. A strongly unstable air mass (MLCAPE forecast to exceed 3000-3500 J/kg in some areas) may also promote an instance or two of marginally severe hail with the most robust cores. One or more Severe Thunderstorm Watches may be needed in the next 1-2 hour to cover this potential
